Council
KOWN-sil
n. (an assembly convened for deliberation or judgment; rendering Greek synedrion)
From Latin concilium, an assembly called together. It is a different word from counsel (Latin consilium, advice), and the KJV keeps them distinct — a council is a body, counsel is what it gives.

Biblical Definition

In the Gospels a council is almost always the Sanhedrin, the seventy-member supreme court of the Jews, and the New Testament's portrait of it is a study in the failure of a lawful institution. The Lord Jesus assumes its authority as ordinary in the Sermon on the Mount, ranking it among real jurisdictions: whoever says Raca to his brother “shall be in danger of the council” (Matthew 5:22). John records the meeting at which it decides His death on frankly political grounds — “Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What do we? for this man doeth many miracles” (John 11:47) — where the miracles are not disputed but treated as a problem. Mark records the trial itself in a sentence that convicts the court rather than the prisoner: “the chief priests and all the council sought for witness against Jesus to put him to death; and found none” (Mark 14:55). A body that seeks witness in order to reach a verdict already decided has ceased to be a court. Acts then shows the same council examining the apostles and being obliged to send them out while it confers, unable to deny the healing done (Acts 4:15). The word passed into church usage for the great ecumenical assemblies — Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon — whose creeds the dictionary affirms without reservation.

Webster 1828 Definition

An assembly for deliberation or judgment — in the Gospels, the Sanhedrin. It decides Christ's death over undisputed miracles, seeks witness to justify a verdict already reached, and cannot deny the apostles' healing.

expand to see more

COUNCIL, n. [L. concilium.] An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.

2. A body of men specially designated to advise a chief magistrate in the administration of the government.

3. An assembly of prelates and doctors, convened for regulating matters of doctrine and discipline in the church.

4. The great council of the Jews was called the Sanhedrim, consisting of seventy elders.

5. Act of deliberation; consultation of a council. Council is not to be confounded with counsel, advice.

Key Scripture

Mark 14:55 — "And the chief priests and all the council sought for witness against Jesus to put him to death; and found none."

John 11:47 — "Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What do we? for this man doeth many miracles."

Matthew 5:22 — "But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire."

Acts 4:15 — "But when they had commanded them to go aside out of the council, they conferred among themselves,"

Modern Corruption

Church councils are treated either as infallible — binding the conscience alongside Scripture — or as worthless, so that a Christian may hold Nicaea and Chalcedon as optional opinions; both errors misplace where authority actually sits.

expand to see more

Rome resolves the question of authority by locating infallibility in the church's councils and its head, so that conciliar definitions bind the conscience with the force of Scripture. The New Testament's own portrait of the highest council available — a lawfully constituted body, with genuine authority, condemning the Son of God on procured testimony — is a permanent argument against the premise. So is the record of church councils since: assemblies have contradicted one another, and the Second Council of Ephesus in 449 was so disgraceful that history calls it the Robber Synod. The confessional position is stated plainly in the 1689: councils and synods may err, and many have erred; therefore they are not to be made the rule of faith, but a help in both.

The opposite error is now more common among evangelicals: since councils can err, they may be ignored, and each believer works out the doctrine of the Trinity from his own reading. The result is a steady rediscovery of ancient heresies by men who have never heard their names — modalism preached from pulpits as an illustration of the Trinity, subordinationism defended as biblical, the two natures of Christ blurred in ordinary devotional speech. Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon are not a second canon; they are the church's accumulated reading of the canon at the points where it was tested hardest, and a man who sets them aside is not being more biblical than the fathers, only less instructed. The dictionary affirms those four councils and their creeds without reservation, as subordinate standards under Scripture alone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek synedrion (a sitting together, hence a council — the Sanhedrin); Hebrew has no exact equivalent, though sod (a confidential council) is used of God's own assembly in Psalm 89:7 and Jeremiah 23:18.

expand to see more

Greek synedrion (G4892) — a council, the Sanhedrin; from syn (together) and hedra (a seat).

Greek symboulion (G4824) — a consultation, plan taken in council; the word in Matthew 12:14 and 27:1.

Hebrew sod (H5475) — a council, intimate circle; used of the counsel of the LORD in Jeremiah 23:18, which the false prophets never stood in.

Hebrew edah (H5712) — a congregation, assembly; the Old Testament gathering with judicial functions.

Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly called out; the church's own word, distinct from synedrion.

Usage

"“Sought for witness… and found none” — a court seeking testimony to support a verdict already reached."

"“What do we? for this man doeth many miracles” — the miracles undisputed and treated as a problem."

"“Commanded them to go aside out of the council” — the highest court in Israel, conferring in private about a healing it cannot deny."
